title: Temu vs Markaz: Which Is Better for Buyers in Pakistan?
summary: Temu vs Markaz in Pakistan: how each compares on payment, landed cost, delivery time and returns, and which to use for what you are buying.
body_markdown:
If you are buying for yourself in Pakistan, Markaz is the more practical of the two: you pay cash on delivery in rupees, and a local courier brings the parcel to your door. Temu has the wider catalogue and the lower sticker prices, but it was never built around how Pakistan pays or receives. Checkout wants an international card, prices are quoted in a foreign currency, and the parcel crosses a border before it reaches you — which adds weeks and a customs question nobody answers at checkout.


That is the short version. The full answer depends on what you are buying, how soon you need it, and what happens if the wrong thing turns up. Below, the two are compared on the five things that actually decide a purchase — payment, real cost, waiting time, recourse and resale — rather than on feature lists.


## The question that settles most of it: how do you want to pay?


Start here, because it disqualifies one option for a lot of people before any other comparison matters.


### Temu: card first


Temu's checkout expects a card that works for international transactions. Many Pakistani debit cards ship with international payments switched off by default, and turning them on means a bank visit, a limit, or both. The workarounds people share — borrowing a relative's card, a wallet top-up, asking someone else to order for you — all put a third person between you and your money. And you pay in full before anything ships.


### Markaz: cash on delivery in rupees


On Markaz you can pay when the parcel reaches you. No card, no advance transfer, no currency conversion to work out afterwards. That is not a small convenience in Pakistan — cash on delivery is how most of the country buys online, and it is a trust mechanism as much as a payment method. You see the box before the money leaves your hand.


If paying in advance to a platform with no local presence is not something you want to do, the comparison ends here. If you are comfortable with card payment, keep reading, because the next four points still move the answer.


## Sticker price versus landed cost


The number on a cross-border listing is not the number you pay. Treat any Temu price as incomplete until three more things are added to it.


**Shipping.** Sometimes free at a threshold, sometimes not, and the free tier usually means the slowest route.


**Duty and taxes.** A cross-border parcel can attract customs charges depending on the item, its declared value and how it travels. You often learn the amount when the courier is already outside your gate.


**Card and currency costs.** Paying in a foreign currency means a conversion, and cards commonly add their own charge on top. It is small per order and it is real.


Markaz quotes one price in PKR and it is the price you pay. For anything in the[Markaz China](https://www.markaz.app/china) catalogue, freight and customs are handled before the product ever reaches you, so the import maths is not your problem. That is the honest trade: a Temu listing can look cheaper than the same category on Markaz, and after shipping, duty and conversion it frequently is not. Compare landed cost against landed cost, not sticker against sticker.


## Delivery: what you are actually waiting for


A cross-border parcel makes four separate journeys — from the seller to a consolidation point in China, out of China, into Pakistan, then across Pakistan to you. Each leg has its own queue, and customs clearance is the one leg nobody can promise a date for. This is why tracking on cross-border orders often goes quiet for a stretch in the middle. Nothing is wrong; the parcel is simply between systems.


Markaz splits the same problem in two. Products stocked in Pakistan are delivered in roughly 3–5 days, because there is no border in the route at all. China-sourced products on Markaz take about 10–17 days, with the freight and clearance already arranged. Neither is instant, but both are a date you can plan around.


The practical rule: if you need it this week, buy something already in Pakistan. Browse[the Markaz catalogue](https://www.markaz.app/shop) first and only go cross-border when nothing local fits. If the wait is fine and the price matters more, the managed China route gives you the factory price without the customs guesswork.


## When something arrives wrong


This is the dimension most comparisons skip, and it is where the gap is widest.


A return to a cross-border platform means shipping the item back out of the country. For anything under a few thousand rupees, the postage and the effort are worth more than the product, so most people keep the wrong item and quietly absorb the loss. There is no local office to visit, no number that reaches a person in your time zone, and any refund arrives back on the card that paid — assuming the claim is accepted.


Markaz runs the after-sale locally: a 7-day return window, buyer protection on the order, and support in the country the parcel was delivered in. For a low-value item that is often the entire difference between a bad purchase and a fixed one.


Ask the question before you order, not after: if this arrives broken, in the wrong size, or not as pictured, what do I actually do on Monday morning?


## Buying one thing versus buying to resell


Buying for yourself, the calculation above is the whole story. Buying to sell on, a third factor appears — your customer's expectations become your constraints.


Reselling from a cross-border app means you pay up front, wait weeks, and then ask a Pakistani customer to either wait with you or pay in advance to a person they have never met. Most will not. You end up funding stock, carrying the delivery risk, and absorbing every return yourself. That is the part that rarely survives contact with a real order —[how Temu works in Pakistan, and what to use instead](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/temu-in-pakistan-how-it-works-shipping-alternatives) walks through it in detail.


Markaz was built the other way round for sellers. There is no minimum order, so you can list a product without buying stock. Your customer pays cash on delivery, and delivery and returns are handled for you. The[Markaz reseller app](https://www.markaz.app/reseller-pk) and the[dropshipping portal](https://www.markaz.app/dropshipping-portal) are the two ways in, depending on whether you are selling from your phone or running a store.


So the answer changes with the question. For a personal purchase it is about payment and recourse. For a business it is about who carries the cash and the risk.


## A category-by-category call


Neither platform is better at everything. Broken down by what people actually put in a cart:


### Fashion and accessories


Sizing is the whole risk, and sizing is exactly what a cross-border return handles worst. Buy locally where you can send it back, or use a route with a local return window. If you want the cross-border comparison on clothing specifically,[Shein in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/shein-in-pakistan) covers the same trade-off for the platform most people are really asking about.


### Home and kitchen


Bulky, breakable, and the categories where duty and shipping eat the price advantage fastest. A managed import or local stock usually wins on landed cost, not just on convenience.


### Gadgets and small electronics


The one place cross-border pricing is genuinely tempting, because the items are light. Weigh it against warranty: a product with no local seller behind it has no local warranty either. For accessories and low-value electronics the risk is small; for anything you depend on daily, it is not.


### Beauty and personal care


Check expiry dates and be careful with anything applied to skin from a seller you cannot identify. Shipping time matters more here than the price gap, and a shorter, traceable route is worth paying for. The[Markaz China categories](https://www.markaz.app/china/categories) are a reasonable place to compare the same items on a managed route.


## Pick in thirty seconds


Choose **Markaz** if any of these is true:


- You want to pay cash on delivery, or you do not have a card enabled for international payments.
- You need the item within the week.
- You want a return window and a local person to talk to if it goes wrong.
- You are buying to resell and do not want to pay for stock up front.


Choose **Temu** if all of these are true:


- You are comfortable paying by card, in advance, in a foreign currency.
- You can wait several weeks and treat the delivery date as approximate.
- The item is cheap enough that you would shrug off a bad one rather than return it.
- You have checked the landed cost — with shipping, duty and card charges — and it is still lower.


For a three-way version of this comparison including Shein, see[Markaz vs Temu vs Shein in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/markaz-vs-temu-vs-shein-pakistan) . If you are still trying to work out whether Temu even ships here properly, start with[is Temu available in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/is-temu-available-in-pakistan) .


## How ordering from Markaz works


1. Open the app or the website and search the category you want. There is an image search on the China catalogue if you have a photo but not a product name.
2. Check the delivery estimate on the listing — locally stocked items run about 3–5 days, China-sourced items about 10–17.
3. Place the order with no minimum quantity. One unit is a valid order.
4. Choose cash on delivery and pay the courier when the parcel arrives.
5. If something is wrong, raise it inside the 7-day return window rather than waiting.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is Temu available in Pakistan?


Not in the way it operates in markets where it has launched properly. Orders sometimes go through, but shoppers hit card-only checkout, foreign-currency pricing, slow cross-border shipping and parcels that can be held at customs. Seeing Temu ads is not the same as Temu being set up to serve you here.


### Can I pay cash on delivery on Temu?


No. Cross-border platforms want payment before dispatch, because the parcel leaves their control the moment it ships. Cash on delivery needs a local operation behind it, which is why platforms that import first — Markaz among them — can offer it and cross-border apps cannot.


### Is Markaz cheaper than Temu?


On sticker price a cross-border listing is often lower. On landed cost the gap narrows or reverses once shipping, duty and card conversion are counted, and it reverses further if the item has to go back. Compare the final rupee number at your door, and count the risk of a return you cannot make.


### Will I be charged customs on a Temu order?


You might. Duty and taxes on a cross-border parcel depend on the item, its declared value and the route, and they are often collected on delivery. That is the charge that turns a cheap order into an average one. Markaz China orders have freight and customs handled before the product reaches you, so there is nothing to settle at the door.


### How long does Markaz delivery take?


Products already stocked in Pakistan arrive in roughly 3–5 days. China-sourced products on Markaz take about 10–17 days, with the import side arranged for you.


### Can I resell products I buy on Temu?


You can, but the economics are hard: you pay in advance, wait weeks, and then need a Pakistani customer to accept that wait or pay up front. A no-minimum-order reseller platform with cash on delivery removes both problems, which is why most sellers here end up on one.


### Do I need a minimum order on Markaz?


No. One unit is a valid order, which is what makes testing a product affordable before committing to a category.


### What if I want the widest possible choice?


A global cross-border app will always list more items. The question is how many of them you can actually receive, pay for and return without friction. If catalogue depth is the priority and you have ruled out the payment problem, compare alternatives properly —[the best AliExpress alternative in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/best-aliexpress-alternative-in-pakistan) lines the options up side by side.
